book: 144 - Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There

chapters.relation: Melancon weighs the Fleet leadership's secrets and lies: Adama's false claim to know the way to Earth, concealing that Cylons look human, Roslin faking Hera's death and hiding the baby, and Zarek's secret collaboration courts on New Caprica. He argues that keeping secrets from the Cylons can be justified by the state's duty to protect, but the leadership repeatedly deceives the governed themselves, discarding the transparency democratic legitimacy requires. Deontological duty to the governed keeps losing to consequentialist reasoning, and the chapter asks what happens to Colonial democracy's 'soul' when trust between government and governed erodes.

chapters.file: ch31 - Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t.md
chapters.relation: McHenry reads the re-imagined series as a holy-war allegory in which both sides weaponize religion, then asks whether that manipulation is ever moral. Adama's lie about Earth is Machiavellian statecraft (with Foucault's point that privileged knowledge holds power), yet defended as serving the greater good, while Roslin's Pythia-based campaign contrasts with Bush's faith-based fear politics. The Cylons emerge as evangelical fundamentalists whose conversion of Baltar through inner Number Six runs on fear, exactly what Madison's case for religious liberty forbids. The chapter concludes the show's own gods have sided with the Colonials.

Muir argues the 1978 original was serious political allegory rather than Moore's 'popcorn': Adar's armistice with the Cylons stands in for Carter-era detente and the SALT treaties, and the sneak attack dramatizes hard-right fears of unilateral disarmament. Adama's 'preparedness' and Sire Uri's disarmament proposal map onto the 'Peace through Strength' doctrine that carried Reagan to power, and 'Experiment in Terra' repeats the lesson as Apollo tells Terra's politicians the opposite of war is slavery, not peace. The chapter notes Soviet Izvestia read it the same way, and that the original thereby fulfilled Moore's own criterion of relevant science fiction from the opposite end of the political spectrum, including Apollo's wartime argument that dissent weakens Colonial resolve.

chapters.file: ch33 - MODEL FIVE - Finding Purpose in the Void.md

chapters.relation: Martinon reads '33' as a phenomenology of temporality under exile: with sunrise, history, and open future gone, the fleet's existence becomes eschatological 'bare life' (following Agamben), sandwiched between the death of the Colonies and death at Cylon hands every thirty-three minutes. The FTL jump figures Derrida's messianic 'to-come' - an undecidable advent that may be salvation or destruction - while the Vipers' obsession with speed narrows life to the next possibility, in a Heideggerian shift from cultural to ontological questioning of death. The episode stays undecidable between Number Six's fatalism ('God is watching out for you, Gaius') and Baltar's contingency, with a birth aboard the fleet - Roslin's smile - as the one open future.

Milburn uses Dewey's account of habit, impulse, and inquiry to explain how the humans navigate: Adama's blocked plans (the decommissioning) are reoriented into a new 'end-in-view' (Earth), and the fleet continuously reformulates its route from scriptures, star charts, pulsars, and the Tomb of Athena constellations as interchangeable signs. The Cylons by contrast cannot revise - Boomer's peace initiative gets her model boxed, and even Cavil's admissions of error lead back to the same path - because they locate their plan in God rather than in constructed, revisable inquiry, needing Baltar even to interpret the signs to Earth. On Deweyan grounds the chapter concludes the humans are never lost while the Cylons are.

chapters.file: ch36 - Free to Be You and Me.md
chapters.relation: Barker reconciles Cylon programming with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's 'intelligible character': Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama and her betrayal of the Cylons to save Tyrol both flow from one innate, conflicted character, just as Baltar's cowardly 'conversion' to the Cylon god expresses his opportunism. Tigh's decision to keep serving after learning he is a Cylon ('My name is Saul Tigh; I am an officer in the colonial fleet') shows character unchanged by revelation. Starbuck's 'special destiny' in 'Maelstrom' is reread not as fate but as her own character - mother-induced self-doubt at war with pilot confidence - which she finally accepts in the vortex; freedom is not freedom from programming but the necessity of manifesting who one already is.

chapters.file: ch37 - Taking in the View from the Paranoid Position.md
chapters.relation: Christian reads the fleet through Freud's death instinct and Melanie Klein's paranoid position: Starbuck's self-destruction, Tigh and Ellen's sadomasochism, and Baltar's relationship with Six fuse Eros and Thanatos, and 'Maelstrom' returns Starbuck to the abusive mother whose rejection of her love taught her that love itself is poisonous. Humans project all aggression and badness onto the Cylons they created - 'toaster' talk, Cain's torture of Gina - to keep a split between good self and evil other. The price is permanent vigilance in the watchtower: since anyone might be a Cylon (the Chief's fear, Baltar's test), the crew can never be sure the projected badness is not their own, which is why the machines must keep 'coming back.'

Vessey asks whether the humanoid Cylons' resurrection makes meaningful life impossible. Humans can aim at a 'successful death' - Socrates drinking the hemlock, the Greek warrior accepting his moira - in which dying completes a life understood as a whole oriented to something larger; a Cylon's death is a mere reset (download), and the exceptions available, dying out of range of a resurrection ship or D'Anna's boxing, occur only through failure or shame and so cannot contribute to meaning. Plato's Symposium link of children to immortality is inverted, since Cylons can only have mortal human-Cylon babies; what separates the Cylons from Sisyphus is not purpose but the option to opt out, which mortality forces on humans and resurrection denies the Cylons.

chapters.file: ch39 - MODEL SIX - Near the End of Our Journey.md

chapters.relation: Wolfe argues the original series is 'deeply Mormon' in ontology though not in epistemology: Kobol anagrams Kolob, the Quorum of Twelve and 'sealing' marriages mirror LDS structure, and the Beings of Light's 'as you are now, we once were; as we are now, you may become' restates Lorenzo Snow's deification couplet, while Count Iblis, like the Mormon Satan, can only rule those who freely yield - agency is supreme. Because none of this is required to follow the show, later licensees could rebuild the metaphysics: the Maximum Press comics incoherently (free will violated when inconvenient), Richard Hatch's novels with a new pure-blood-of-Kobol cosmology, and Ronald Moore with a circular 'all this has happened before' replacing eternal progression.

Berger deploys Bakhtin's dialogism to answer the 'GINO' charge: the re-imagined series is not a betrayal of Larson's show but a heteroglossic utterance in an ongoing conversation that already included the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greco-Roman myth, and later fanfic and blogs, with each version sourcing its sources' sources. The 2003 series is read as polyphonic about belief: skeptic Adama, devout Number Six, the messianic convert Baltar, and Dawkins/Hitchens-style atheist critiques of fundamentalism are all given equal voice. The show's value lies in inviting debate across the whole continuum of belief rather than preaching a position.

The chapter locates the real fan schism in worldview: the original series is Manichaean moral absolutism - Count Iblis and the Ships of Light wage a cosmic Light/Darkness war in which Evil is one force (Iblis sharing the Imperious Leader's voice) and humanity is the battleground - while Moore's re-imagining is Protagorean relativism ('man is the measure'), where right depends entirely on context. Evidence: Roslin abandons the FTL-less ships as 'a matter of numbers' yet burns forty-three percent of fuel reserves to find Starbuck; Leoben is airlocked after Starbuck's interrogation while Thorne is killed for torturing Athena; producer Eick even defends Caprica Six's killing of the baby as possibly a mercy. The two shows thus embody absolutist nostalgia for moral clarity versus post-9/11 moral ambiguity.

Kirkland argues BSG imagines gender-free institutions (unisex heads and quarters, Starbuck never having to justify fighting) while installing a default masculinity under Adama, so that feminine-coded women die: Ellen the femme fatale is poisoned, pilots Kat and Kendra earn redemption only through death, and Cain's female command is written as militarist nightmare aligned with Gina's sexual abuse. Starbuck confounds the sexualizing male gaze and reverses rescue narratives, and 'The Farm' plus her captivity with Leoben on New Caprica literalize feminist critiques of patriarchal medicine and compulsory heterosexuality. Yet she is masculinized, pathologized via her abusive mother, brought to submit to Leoben as spiritual guide, and killed in 'Maelstrom' - containing the transgressive heroine within the show's patriarchy.

chapters.file: ch44 - Human, Machine, or Something In-between.md
chapters.relation: Rolufs maps Genesis' Eve onto Boomer (who shoots Adama without understanding her act, as Eve could not know betrayal before eating the fruit) and onto Caprica Six (whose fall required Baltar's Adam-like blame-shifting), and the Zohar's Lilith - seductress, child-killer, seeker of equality - onto Six's red dresses and neck-snapping and Sharon's sexual dominance of Helo. Both Cylon women are compromised figures who love the humans they betrayed, and their ambiguity between human and machine mirrors the ambiguity between woman and demon in the myths. Through them the chapter argues pop culture redeems Eve and Lilith from misogynistic readings: Six's killing of the baby becomes possibly merciful, and the first women get the chance at redemption the myths denied them.

This fan-fiction interlude dramatizes the fandom debate aboard Galactica: Roslin voices the Frankfurt School view (a 'Scorpion School' of Adorno and Benjamin - mass culture as mindless absorption, reproduction destroying the artwork's aura), while aide Billy cites Henry Jenkins and Textual Poachers to defend fanzines as participatory culture repairing corporate ownership of myth, and a fan meeting wins the President over as community-building. Baltar and inner Number Six extend the argument: Six demands 'the singular truth of the show' against fan rewriting, and Baltar answers that the Cylons are themselves a fanfiction of the human brain - twelve unoriginal faces. Starbuck is revealed as the anonymous fanfic writer.

The chapter introduces Wayne Booth's 'coduction' - ethical criticism of fiction validated by comparing one's reasoned judgments with other qualified readers in ongoing, open-minded conversation - and argues Battlestar is a highly ethical show not because its characters behave well but because it invites coduction: the abortion-under-extinction, torture, and New Caprica suicide-bombing plots (Baltar cornering Roslin, who cannot justify the bombings) open discussion instead of preaching, the mark of art rather than propaganda. Rules for genuine coduction follow - treat Iraq as one applicability among several occupations, stay informed, remain open to changing your mind - with Ron Moore's blog exchange on the absence of gay characters as the model case, and the book itself offered as one contribution to the continuing conversation.

chapters.file: ch54 - The Universe is a vast and complex system coincidental, serendipitous events.md

holes.name: Giorgio Agamben
holes.what: Italian philosopher best known for homo sacer and 'bare life' - human existence reduced to biological survival stripped of political meaning under sovereign power.
holes.why: Chapter 34 explicitly follows Agamben to describe the fleet in '33' as bare life suspended between two deaths, cut off from history and future.

holes.name: Melanie Klein
holes.what: Psychoanalyst who placed the death instinct at the center of infant development, explaining anxiety through splitting, projection, and the paranoid position.
holes.why: Chapter 37 uses Klein's paranoid position and projection as its central lens: humans project aggression onto the Cylons and must stand perpetual watch for its return.

holes.name: Mormon Theology (LDS cosmology)
holes.what: Latter-day Saint doctrines - Kolob, eternal progression, deification, uncreated matter, and absolute moral agency - teaching that humans may become as God is.
holes.why: Chapter 40 argues the original series' whole ontology (Kobol, Quorum of Twelve, sealing, the Beings of Light) is built from creator Glen Larson's Mormon theology.

holes.name: Mikhail Bakhtin
holes.what: Russian theorist of the dialogic: texts speak in polyphonic dialogue (heteroglossia) with other voices and texts rather than standing as single-authored works.
holes.why: Chapter 41 answers the 'GINO' charge with Bakhtin's dialogism, reading the re-imagined series as one polyphonic utterance in conversation with Mormon, mythic, and fan sources.

holes.name: Mani
holes.what: Third-century Persian founder of Manichaeism, a dualist religion of perpetual war between the forces of Light and Darkness with humanity as the battleground.
holes.why: Chapter 42 reads the original series' moral absolutism - Count Iblis versus the Ships of Light - as Manichaean cosmology set against the remake's relativism.

holes.name: Eve and Lilith Myths
holes.what: Genesis and rabbinic narratives (Zohar, Alphabet of Ben Sira) of the first women: Eve the transgressing mother of humanity and Lilith the demonized equal who refused subordination to Adam.
holes.why: Chapter 44 maps Cylons Six and Sharon onto Eve and Lilith in order to redeem both the demonized myths and the characters from misogynistic readings.

holes.name: Coduction (ethical criticism of fiction)
holes.what: Wayne Booth's method of ethical criticism: validating one's judgment of a fiction by comparing reasons with other qualified readers in ongoing, open-minded conversation.
holes.why: Chapter 46 argues Battlestar is an ethical show because it invites coduction about abortion, torture, and suicide bombing rather than closing down discussion.
